units.en: A ⟦0⟧ is a nation that is more or less controlled by another, often stronger nation, through an installed government that is loyal to the controlling nation.

When a country is puppeted, its government is replaced by one installed by the puppet master, matching the puppet master's ideology. If a puppet master declares war, they can call in their puppets as allies. In the ⟦0⟧ that ensues after a successful war, puppeted countries will not be able to make demands by themselves (except for high autonomy level puppets such as dominions and satellites), though the puppet master can dictate demands in favor of its puppets if they choose to do so. As a result, an already puppeted country cannot puppet other countries.

If a puppet master is forced to capitulate, its puppets will automatically capitulate as well if they aren't in a faction with a major country that has yet to capitulate. If a puppet master capitulates but there are still majors in a puppet's faction, the puppet will earn autonomy points. Upon defeating a puppet master (and other majors in faction with it), the victorious nations can choose to detach puppeted countries from their puppet master, making them free-standing nations again. Communist countries get a 35% cost reduction for puppeting other countries.

The puppet master nation may ⟦0⟧ goods from its puppet or subject state at a rate discounted below the standard trade rate of up to 8 loads of a resource per factory. For example, puppet or an integrated puppet, such as Malaya, provides 80 loads per factory to its British master (90% discount), while a colony (British Raj) offers 16 loads (50% discount) and British dominions offer 10 loads per factory (25% discount).

The puppet master may access far more of the puppet's resources than it could otherwise with its own trade laws if directly annexed. Extra Trade for overlord provides a bonus on top of the puppet's Trade Law to market rate. So if a Puppet would have 200 ⟦0⟧ available and has ⟦1⟧, typically, only 80% of their resources go to export (160 ⟦2⟧) the rest can be kept for themselves. With the Extra trade bonus of +25% (from Dominion level autonomy) this brings the total ⟦3⟧ available to export from a puppet to 170 (160 + 10, where 10 is 25% of 40, where 40 is 200 - 160) out of their total of 200. This can mean with Integrated Puppets the puppet master may purchase all of their resources even if they switch to ⟦4⟧. The extra trade to overlord is applied to the resources not exported.

Integrated Puppets, Reichskommissariats/Reichsprotektorates and Imperial Associates/Protectorates give a small share of their civilian factories (incl. refineries) and a major share of their military factories to the puppet master. Naval dockyards are unaffected. See charts for details.

At certain levels of autonomy a puppet master may request license production of a puppet's equipment, at a discount or even completely free. In addition to being given access to equipment without needing to research it, there is also a bonus conferred to researching that equipment while the license is in effect. Speeding up research for domestic equipment.
It is possible to "request" control over the troops of the puppet; this provides additional divisions for the puppet master, although puppet divisions may not be very well designed.

When doing so, it is desirable for the player to ⟦0⟧ appropriate equipment to the puppet nation which will allow for faster division training as well as combat any existing puppet equipment shortages. Alternatively, the master may request lend-lease equipment from the puppet to drain its equipment stocks. Puppet can still receive lend-lease from countries other than the puppet's master - and puppet, most likely, will ask others for equipment, as it usually has equipment shortages, and often has little-to-no industry. Then, puppet master can request lend-lease equipment from puppet, to drain puppet's stocks. Puppet and puppet master have separate lend-lease cooldowns. Therefore, puppet master can use puppet to beg equipment from other factions.

Then, puppet master can request lend-lease equipment from puppet, to drain puppet's stocks. Puppet and puppet master have separate lend-lease cooldowns. Therefore, puppet master can use puppet to beg equipment from other factions.

The master can effectively boost their own manpower by raising units including a mix of master and puppet manpower (70% for a Colony, 90% for a Puppet, and 100% for an Integrated Puppet). Such colonial divisions are controlled by the puppet master. The templates for such colonial divisions are those taken or adapted from the puppet's own template list (open by clicking the Crown icon at the top of the Division Designer in the Recruit/Deploy menu). If a puppet is newly released, it will receive templates of the puppet master.
Puppet can send garrison support to save up on manpower.
Puppet doesn't need garrison - what allows to save up on manpower and weapons.

Puppeting countries can often be safer than annexing them as it generates less World Tension than territorial annexation, reducing the risk of foreign intervention by other potentially hostile countries.
Puppeting allows countries to retain any fleets. As capital ships take a long time to construct, this can drastically aid naval supremacy.
Communist countries can puppet defeated nations at a 10% discount in peace deals, allowing them to put more territory under their (indirect) control after a war.
Some puppet autonomy levels will transfer some of their war score to their overlord.
With ⟦0⟧ DLC, Satellites, Dominions, Imperial Subjects, and Supervised States can contribute spies to a spymaster.
Puppets can research different technologies than his Puppet Master. Then, Puppet Master and Puppets can share their research with each other, ⟦0⟧.
using Technology sharing and Equipment licensing

Master's divisions can get resupplied from puppet's logistics network if they are on puppet's territory. If master's underequipped divisions are stationed on puppet's territory, it will allow to arm said divisions at the expense of puppet, which doesn't increase puppet's autonomy. Similarly, some pieces of master's equipment may end up in possession of puppet's divisions if puppet's divisions move to master's territory.

There's also a weird "non-existent puppet" or "virtual puppet" bug. If you release a puppet, all currently controlled states of which are your cores (e.g. ⟦0⟧ for ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧ for France), while keeping cores, puppet is technically released but doesn't receive any states. This results in puppet existing only "on paper", without physical representation on map; so much as ⟦3⟧ them requires quick double-click in Open Country List. Such non-existent puppets do give small benefits, as they do their own research, but do clutter the interface.

It's also possible to drain weapons via rump state Puppet. When conquering a country, ideally with lots of weapons, in Peace Conference annex all States of country except the most worthless one, and make the conquered country a Puppet while only leaving that one state for them. Then, order Puppet to give you their equipment via lend-lease - getting access to the other half of their arsenal which you didn't recieve upon capitulating the country. Eventually after a very long while, the rump states becomes independent again, at which point it can be conquered again or just ignored.

On one hand, if you release Puppet earlier, it will have more time to complete it's focus tree, construct buildings, field divisions and beg others for lend-lease. On the other side, newly released puppet will receive templates of the puppet master - so, if you're planning to use Puppet for war (be it colonial divisions, or divisions of puppet you "requested" control), you should consider ⟦0⟧. Also, many Puppets have less research slots than their masters - so, if they get released more early, then they will be less technologically advanced in the long run (not a big problem).
making all needed, battle-ready templates before releasing Puppet

Puppeting small countries with few resources is less efficient than simply annexing the country, especially if the puppet has less than 8 but more than 0 units of the resource, as factories still have to be paid. If the would-be puppet country is conquered, the problem can be greatly postponed by Resource Rights Demands.
If the would-be puppet country is conquered, the problem can be greatly postponed by ⟦0⟧.
If you give too much land to a puppet, it may refuse to give you your land back.
Puppets can receive lend lease from their master, even in peacetime. This may help in multiplayer games to grant a puppet a head-start in multiplayer games with a 1936 start date.
Puppets generally can receive lend lease from their master at a lower tension level than normal.

If a nation declares war on a puppet, its master will automatically turn hostile towards the nation that declared war on it and join the war, bringing them as well as all their other puppets into the fight.
A puppet receives a reduced number of factories for giving resources to its master. This can hinder early-game industry development.

A puppet can neither justify war goals nor can it declare war on another country, in addition to that, puppets cannot make demands in a peace conference, meaning that a puppet's territorial expansion is entirely decided by the puppet master.

If a puppet master declares war on a nation, they can freely force the puppet into the war (Imperial Subjects can decline it). If matched up against a stronger opponent and fighting alone, the odds are clearly not in its favor. Even if the puppet proves stronger and defeats that enemy, it gets nothing but glory (and autonomy points) from the war unless the puppet master provides something in the peace or thereafter.

A puppet has to deal with autonomy or risk further disadvantages in favor of its overlord or, at worst, direct annexation by its overlord. One of the quickest and most reliable ways to raise autonomy is to use a continuous focus, wasting time that could be used for completing other national focuses. A puppet may also gain autonomy by trading or lend-leasing goods to its overlord. However, puppets with unique focus trees usually have a national focus that is even quicker than said method.

Some puppets are more independent than others. To represent the difference between largely autonomous dominions like Canada, somewhat autonomous colonies like the British Raj, and totally subservient puppet states like Malaya, the game divides subject states into four levels of autonomy. Within each level, ⟦0⟧ has a numerical level between 0 and 1000.

At 1000 ⟦0⟧, the subject may advance to a higher tier, or become free if it is already a ⟦1⟧. At 0 autonomy, the master may decrease autonomy to a lower tier, or annex the puppet entirely if it is already an ⟦2⟧. Changing tiers costs 50 ⟦3⟧, while annexing a subject costs 300 ⟦4⟧ and becoming free costs 300 ⟦5⟧.⟦6⟧
